items.title: Why the marathon is 26.2 miles
items.claim: The modern marathon distance of 26 miles 385 yards (42.195 km) was set in which year?

options.text: 490 BCE (Battle of Marathon)
London 1908 Olympics
Athens 1896 Olympics
Tokyo 1964

items.reveal_title: Set in 1908 to suit a royal viewing arrangement
items.reveal:
The London 1908 course was extended so the start at Windsor Castle and the finish at the royal box in White City stadium gave a distance of 26 miles 385 yards. The IAAF adopted it as standard in 1921.

Earlier modern marathons varied between about 25 and 26 miles.
items.why: Athletic standards often have administrative rather than scientific origins.

items.title: Lactate is not metabolic waste
items.claim: For decades lactic acid was described as the cause of muscle fatigue and post-exercise soreness. What does current physiology say?

options.text: Lactate directly causes delayed onset muscle soreness
Lactate is an important metabolic fuel, recycled to glucose and used by tissues
It has no role in metabolism
It is only present at rest

items.reveal_title: Lactate is a fuel, not a waste product
items.reveal:
Brooks's lactate shuttle hypothesis (1986, refined since) describes lactate produced in one tissue being transported to and oxidised by others, or recycled to glucose in the liver (Cori cycle).

Delayed onset muscle soreness is now attributed to micro-damage and inflammation, not lactate.
items.why: Sport-science textbooks lagged decades behind physiological evidence in changing this terminology.

items.title: Title IX participation increase
items.claim: Title IX of the US Education Amendments (1972) banned sex discrimination in federally funded education, including athletics. By 2018, what proportion of US high school athletes were girls compared with 1971?

options.text: Roughly the same
Roughly 10x more (about 295,000 in 1971 versus over 3 million by the 2010s)
Down by half
Now zero

items.reveal:
National Federation of State High School Associations data show girls' high school athletic participation rising from around 295,000 in 1971-72 to over 3.4 million in 2018-19.

Funding and facility disparities persist; the legal framework changed participation faster than parity.
items.why: Single policy interventions can reshape participation across decades.

items.title: First modern Olympics
items.claim: Approximately how many athletes competed at the first modern Olympics in Athens 1896?

options.text: Around 240 athletes from 14 nations
Around 10,000 from 200 nations
Around 50,000 from 50 nations
Around 25 athletes

items.reveal:
Sources vary from around 241 to 280 athletes from roughly 14 nations.

Women first competed at Paris 1900 (in tennis, golf and a few other sports).
items.why: The scale of contemporary Olympics is not built in; it grew from a modest revival.

items.title: Where the Paralympics began
items.claim: The Paralympic movement traces back to which institution and clinician?

options.text: Munich 1972
Stoke Mandeville Hospital, UK, with Ludwig Guttmann's 1948 games for spinal-injured veterans
Helsinki 1952
Sydney 2000

items.reveal:
Guttmann staged archery contests for World War II veterans with spinal cord injuries on the opening day of the London 1948 Olympics.

The first Paralympic Games proper were held in Rome in 1960.
items.why: Para-sport began as a rehabilitative intervention, not a sporting tradition.

items.title: Static stretching before exercise
items.claim: Sports science guidance on pre-exercise static stretching changed substantially. What do current consensus reviews say?

options.text: Static stretching pre-exercise reliably reduces injury and improves performance
Long static holds before power activities can reduce subsequent performance; dynamic warm-up is generally preferred
No warm-up of any kind is recommended
Stretching prevents all injuries

items.reveal_title: Pre-exercise long static holds can hurt power output
items.reveal:
Reviews (Behm and Chaouachi, 2011; Behm et al., 2016) summarise that holds longer than around 60 seconds before sprint or jump activities can transiently reduce performance.

Dynamic warm-ups are now standard in elite team-sport protocols.
items.why: Practice guidelines often persist in coaching long after research has moved on.

items.title: Altitude training paradigm
items.claim: Levine and Stray-Gundersen's 'live high, train low' studies (1997) argued for which protocol?

options.text: Train at low altitude only
Live at altitude (around 2,500 m) to stimulate red-cell production, but train at low altitude to maintain workload
Live and train at sea level
Train only at altitudes above 5,000 m

items.reveal_title: Sleep high, train low to combine adaptation and intensity
items.reveal:
The protocol attempts to gain the haematological benefits of altitude exposure without losing training quality.

Subsequent research and commercial 'altitude tents' aim to replicate the stimulus at any geographical location.
items.why: Elite training innovations often emerge from blending physiology and pragmatic logistics.

items.title: Biological passports
items.claim: WADA introduced the Athlete Biological Passport in 2009 to detect doping. What does it primarily monitor?

options.text: Travel history
Longitudinal changes in biomarkers (e.g. haematological) that suggest manipulation, even without a positive substance test
DNA sequence
Diet

items.reveal:
The passport tracks haematological, steroidal and (more recently) endocrine markers across an athlete's career. Significant deviations can trigger sanctions even without finding the substance itself.

The approach has produced sanctions where direct testing failed.
items.why: Indirect, statistical evidence has become a major tool in anti-doping enforcement.

items.title: CTE and contact sports
items.claim: Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE) is a neurodegenerative condition linked to repeated head impacts. What is true about diagnosis?

options.text: It is reliably diagnosed in life
Definitive diagnosis is currently only possible at post-mortem
It only occurs in boxing
It can be diagnosed by a single blood test

items.reveal:
Mez et al. (2017, JAMA) reported CTE pathology in 110 of 111 deceased NFL players whose brains were examined. The sample was self-selected, but the proportion is striking.

In-life diagnostic biomarkers are an active research area.
items.why: Sport policy operates under uncertainty when the condition cannot be confirmed in living athletes.

items.title: BMI's limits for athletes
items.claim: Body Mass Index (Quetelet, 1830s; popularised in the 20th century) is a single number from mass over height squared. Why is it problematic for athletes?

options.text: It overestimates fitness
It does not distinguish lean mass from fat mass, so muscular athletes are often classified overweight or obese
It varies with the weather
It is unrelated to body shape

items.reveal:
Rugby forwards, weightlifters and bodybuilders routinely fall above the 'overweight' or 'obese' threshold despite low body fat.

DXA, hydrostatic weighing and skinfolds give better composition data for performance contexts.
items.why: Population-level measures and individual measures answer different questions.

items.title: The 10,000-hour rule
items.claim: Anders Ericsson's research on expertise was popularised as a '10,000-hour rule' by Malcolm Gladwell. What did Ericsson himself say about it?

options.text: He coined and endorsed the simple rule
He argued deliberate practice mattered, but rejected the simple hours-to-mastery shorthand
He said hours did not matter at all
He demonstrated 100 hours is sufficient for any sport

items.reveal_title: Ericsson pushed back on the round number
items.reveal:
Ericsson's Peak (2016) and earlier papers emphasised deliberate, structured practice with feedback, and noted that hours alone are insufficient. He criticised the 10,000-hour shorthand.

Macnamara et al. (2014) meta-analysis found practice accounted for variable proportions of expertise depending on domain.
items.why: Popular versions of research findings can outlive the researcher's own corrections.
